title: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
summary: Why final-answer rewards are a weak teacher, how PRMs are trained, built and scored, what a step reward should measure, how PRMs guide search and RL, and where they break.
outcomes: Explain why process supervision gives better credit assignment than outcome supervision, with the PRM800K results
Train a token-classification PRM with labels only on step separators and use it to rerank sampled solutions
Compute Monte Carlo hard and soft step labels and explain why they estimate value, not step correctness
Compute step progress (advantages) and implicit-PRM step rewards, and explain why they beat raw value
Trace PRM-guided beam search, weighted voting and step rewards in GRPO and PPO on small examples
Explain how dense PRM rewards get hacked in RL and how Clip and Delta bound them
Compare discriminative and generative PRMs on cost, labels, calibration and ProcessBench error location

lessons.title: Grading the answer versus grading every step

blocks.md: In the GRPO and RLVR course the reward was a **verifier** on the final answer: 1 if the boxed number matches the reference, 0 otherwise. That signal is cheap and hard to fool on the answer itself, but it says nothing about the steps that produced it. This lesson asks what is lost when only the end of a chain of thought is graded, and what a step-level grader buys back.

Two kinds of learned grader appear throughout. An **outcome reward model (ORM)** reads a whole solution and predicts one number: the probability that the final answer is correct. A **process reward model (PRM)** reads the same solution and predicts a number for **each step**: the probability that this step is correct. The names come from Uesato et al. (DeepMind, 2022), who separated *outcome-based* supervision (labels on the final result) from *process-based* supervision (labels on each reasoning step).

Take a tiny problem: *a shirt costs 40 dollars, is discounted 25%, then taxed 8%. What is the final price?* The correct path is: discount = 10, sale price = 30, tax = 0.08 x 30 = 2.4, total = 32.4. Below are three sampled solutions, each split into four newline-separated steps, and the labels each kind of supervision would give them.

blocks.title: One problem, three solutions, two kinds of label

scenes.caption: Three solutions to the shirt problem, four steps each. The true answer is 32.4. Nothing is graded yet.
Outcome labels: only the last cell is checked against 32.4. Solutions 1 and 3 get label 1, solution 2 gets 0. The ORM learns from one bit per solution.
Process labels on solution 2: steps 1 and 2 are right, step 3 taxes the original price (0.08 x 40 = 3.2) instead of the sale price. The label pinpoints the step that broke.
Solution 3 taxes the wrong base (3.2) and then miscomputes 40 - 10 + 3.2 as 32.4. Two errors cancel. The outcome label says correct; process labels mark step 2 wrong.

blocks.md: Two weaknesses of outcome labels fall out of the example. First, **credit assignment**: a 0 on solution 2 tells the grader that something went wrong somewhere, but not where, so it must infer the location itself. Lightman et al. (OpenAI, 2023) point out that on hard problems most sampled solutions contain an error somewhere, so a negative outcome label carries little information. Second, **false positives**: solution 3 reaches the right number by wrong reasoning, and final-answer checking rewards it.

A correct final answer does not mean correct reasoning. On GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021: about 8,500 grade-school math word problems), Uesato et al. found that RL directly against final-answer correctness left a best **trace error** (any human-judged mistake in the reasoning, among answer-correct solutions) of 12.4%, versus 3.8% for their best process-based method.

Lightman et al. ran the largest comparison. They fine-tuned GPT-4 into an ORM and a PRM and used each for **best-of-N**: sample N solutions from a fixed generator, let the reward model pick the highest-scored one, and check whether its final answer is right. Majority voting (pick the most common final answer) is the baseline that needs no reward model. The test set is MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021), 12,500 high-school competition problems with checkable final answers.

blocks.title: Best-of-N on MATH: PRM vs ORM vs majority vote

scenes.caption: Best-of-1860 on a 500-problem MATH test subset (Lightman et al., 2023). The PRM picks a correct solution for 78.2% of problems; the ORM 72.4%; majority vote 69.6%.

Out of distribution: 224 new AP (Advanced Placement exam) Calculus, Chemistry and Physics plus AMC (American Mathematics Competitions) problems, best-of-100. Aggregate: PRM 72.9%, ORM 63.8%, majority vote 61.3%. The gap survives the shift.

blocks.prompt: Uesato et al. (2022, GSM8K) found that outcome-based and process-based training reached nearly the same **final-answer** error rate. Lightman et al. (2023, MATH) found the PRM clearly better. Both can be true. What changed?
blocks.reveal: Lightman et al. list three differences: a more capable base model (GPT-4), far more human feedback (800K step labels), and the harder MATH dataset instead of grade-school math. They attribute the apparent conflict mainly to scale: their data-scaling curves show a little process supervision matching a lot of outcome supervision, with process supervision pulling ahead as labels grow. Note also that Uesato et al. still found process supervision (or a reward model that emulates it) was needed for low **trace** error.

blocks.md: An ORM gets one label per solution and must discover where errors are. A PRM is told where the first error is. That extra information is why PRMs rank solutions better on hard problems, and why they can reject right answers reached by wrong reasoning.

blocks.question: A generator samples 100 solutions to a hard olympiad problem; 97 have wrong final answers. Why is outcome supervision on this problem a weak training signal for a reward model?
options: Outcome labels are noisy because the answer checker is usually wrong
Almost every label is 0, and a 0 does not say which step failed, so the model learns little about where reasoning breaks
Outcome labels cannot be computed for olympiad problems
The reward model would overfit to the 3 correct solutions and ignore the rest
blocks.explain: When nearly all solutions are wrong, a 0 is the expected label and says only 'some step was wrong'. Lightman et al. make exactly this credit-assignment argument: process labels also say how many leading steps were right and where the first mistake is.

blocks.question: Which solution in the shirt example would an outcome-trained grader be most likely to reward wrongly?
options: Solution 1, because it is long
Solution 2, because its final answer is wrong
Solution 3, because its errors cancel and the final answer matches
blocks.explain: Solution 3 gets outcome label 1 despite two wrong steps. This is the false-positive problem: final-answer checking rewards right answers reached by wrong reasoning, and a reward model trained on those labels can learn to accept such reasoning.

lessons.title: How a PRM is trained and how it scores a solution

blocks.md: A PRM is usually an ordinary language model fine-tuned to emit a judgement at the end of each step. In Lightman et al., the generator writes one step per line. The PRM reads the problem plus solution and, after the last token of each step, predicts a single token meaning *correct* or *incorrect*. Training maximizes the log-likelihood of those label tokens, so it runs in a standard language-model pipeline. At test time **one forward pass** over the whole solution yields every step score at once.

Human labelers gave each step a **positive** (correct and reasonable), **negative** (incorrect or unreasonable) or **neutral** (ambiguous) label. Labels were collected only **up to the first incorrect step**. Lightman et al. chose this to keep the comparison with outcome supervision straightforward (for a correct solution both say *all steps fine*; for a wrong one process supervision additionally says *where*) and to keep labeling cost similar, since without a final answer to check, grading a solution already means finding its first mistake.

blocks.caption: Per-solution PRM loss: cross-entropy on each labeled step. p is the predicted probability that step i is correct, y is 1 for correct, and k is the index of the first incorrect step (or the last step if none). s_i is step i and theta the PRM weights.

blocks.md: In words: a step labeled correct costs $-\log p$, which shrinks toward 0 as the PRM grows confident the step is right; a step labeled wrong costs $-\log(1-p)$, which shrinks as $p$ falls toward 0. This binary cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood of the label tokens, so minimizing it is exactly the log-likelihood training described above. The sum stops at step $k$ because no labels exist after the first error.

The result was **PRM800K**: 800K step-level labels across 75K solutions to 12K MATH problems, released by OpenAI. Labeling was steered by **active learning**: rather than showing labelers random samples, they surfaced *convincing wrong-answer* solutions, ones the current PRM rated highly but whose final answer was wrong. Each such solution is guaranteed to contain a step the PRM misjudged. In small-scale ablations (controlled runs that change one design choice, here how samples are picked, and hold the rest fixed) this was about 2.6x more data-efficient than uniform sampling.

To rank whole solutions the per-step probabilities must be reduced to one number. Three reductions are common: the **product** (probability that every step is correct, assuming independence), the **minimum** (the solution is as good as its weakest step), and the **last step** score. Here are three made-up PRM outputs to compare them.

blocks.title: Three ways to turn step scores into one score

scenes.caption: Step probabilities from a PRM for three solutions (illustrative values). B is long and every step is confident; C has one step the PRM strongly doubts.
Product: A = 0.787, B = 0.97^8 = 0.784, C = 0.162. B loses to A even though each of its steps is more confident. The product penalizes length.
Minimum: A = 0.90, B = 0.97, C = 0.20. Now B ranks first. The minimum ignores length and is driven entirely by the weakest step.
Last step: A = 0.92, B = 0.97, C = 0.90. C nearly ties A despite its bad step 3. This is only safe if the PRM's last score already reflects earlier mistakes.

blocks.prompt: Lightman et al. tried product vs minimum and neutral-as-positive vs neutral-as-negative on best-of-1860. How large do you expect the spread between the best and worst of the four strategies to be?
blocks.reveal: Small: 78.2% (product, neutral = positive) down to 77.4% (product, neutral = negative), with minimum at 77.6% and 77.8%. The authors call the differences minor and note the product's slight bias against longer solutions. Math-Shepherd, an automatically labeled PRM from lesson 4, scores with the minimum. Snell et al. (2024), a study of how to spend compute at test time, found the **last-step** score best for their PRM, whose step scores are trained as reward-to-go: the chance of reaching a correct final answer from that step onward. The last step's value therefore already sums up the whole solution (more in lesson 4).

blocks.title: Lightman et al. Table 4: scoring strategy barely matters

scenes.caption: Best-of-1860 accuracy on their MATH subset under four reductions. The full spread is 0.8 points; the reward model's quality dominates the choice of reduction.

blocks.caption: Scoring a solution with a classifier-style PRM (sketch; step_probs comes from one forward pass).

blocks.md: A PRM is a per-step classifier read off in one forward pass. Training labels stop at the first error. To compare solutions you reduce step scores to one number; product and minimum perform similarly, but product quietly favours shorter solutions.

blocks.question: Your PRM uses the product reduction and keeps choosing terse 2-step solutions over careful 9-step ones that are also correct. What is the most likely cause?
options: The PRM was trained on too few negative labels
Multiplying many probabilities below 1 shrinks the score of long solutions even when each step is confident
The minimum reduction would make the bias worse
Neutral labels were treated as negative
blocks.explain: With p = 0.97 per step, 2 steps give 0.94 but 9 steps give 0.76. The product is a probability that all steps are right under an independence assumption, so it falls with length. Lightman et al. note this bias; minimum or last-step scores avoid it.

blocks.question: Why did Lightman et al. surface 'convincing wrong-answer' solutions to labelers instead of random samples?
options: They are guaranteed to contain a step the current PRM misjudged, so each label corrects a real mistake
They are shorter, so labeling is cheaper
Random samples cannot be split into steps
It removes the need to label correct solutions at all
blocks.explain: A solution the PRM rates highly but whose answer is wrong must contain at least one step the PRM scored too high. Labeling it is maximally informative. This active learning was about 2.6x more data-efficient in their ablation.

lessons.title: Build it: train a small PRM and rerank with it

blocks.md: Lesson 2 described a PRM as a classifier read out at the end of every step. This lesson builds one: a 0.5-billion-parameter PRM trained on Math-Shepherd's automatic step labels, then used to pick among 16 sampled answers to grade-school math problems. Everything here ran on a laptop (an Apple Silicon Mac, using its built-in GPU through PyTorch's MPS backend, no CUDA GPU), so the model and data are small and the numbers are noisy, but every number is real output.

A Math-Shepherd row (the `trl-lib/math_shepherd` copy on Hugging Face, 422,422 training rows) holds a `prompt`, a list of `completions` (the steps, each starting *Step k:*) and one boolean label per step (true if any sampled continuation from that step reached the right answer: the *hard estimation* that lesson 4 explains). Here is a real row with three steps labeled correct, wrong, wrong:

*Mr. Maxwell takes 1 hr to drive to work in the morning but 1 and half hours to drive back home ... what is the average speed of his return journey?*

- Step 1: ... 1+1/2 = 90 minutes to drive home. (labeled correct)
- Step 2: ... a distance of 90/30 = 3 miles. (wrong)
- Step 3: ... average speed for the return journey is 30+3 = 33mph. The answer is: 33 (wrong)

The labels must land on tokens. The recipe (adapted from TRL's experimental `PRMTrainer`, removed from the library in September 2026) ends every step with a **step separator**, here a newline (we also put one after the prompt; TRL did not), and gives every token the label -100 except the separator that ends each step, which gets 1 (correct) or 0 (wrong). In PyTorch's cross-entropy, -100 is the default *ignore index*: those positions contribute no loss. The model is an ordinary language model with its next-token head replaced by a 2-way classification head on every position (`AutoModelForTokenClassification`).

blocks.title: Step labels land only on separator tokens

scenes.caption: Prompt: 2 + 3 times 4. Steps: 3 times 4 = 12 (correct) and 2 + 12 = 14 (wrong), written with an asterisk and tokenized by the Qwen2.5 tokenizer. nl is the newline separator, id 198. Note ?nl: the prompt's question mark and newline merged into one token.
Labels: -100 everywhere (ignored by the loss) except the separator after each step. Step 1's separator gets 1, step 2's gets 0.
At test time, one forward pass gives a 2-way softmax at every position; you read only positions 13 and 21. That is the one-pass scoring of lesson 2.

blocks.md: Tokenize each step separately and append the separator id yourself. In the Qwen2.5 tokenizer a step ending in a period followed by a newline becomes the single token for period-plus-newline (id 624), so tokenizing the joined text gives no separate newline token to read, and the label would sit on a different token than at training time.

blocks.caption: Training script, run here: 4,000 random Math-Shepherd rows, 1 epoch, 500 optimizer steps of 8 rows, about 9 minutes on an Apple Silicon GPU through PyTorch MPS. The run also saved the model for scoring. Note the explicit `features=` in `map`; the next blocks explain why.
blocks.code:
from datasets import load_dataset, Features, Sequence, Value
from transformers import (AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForTokenClassification,
    Trainer, TrainingArguments, DataCollatorForTokenClassification)

BASE = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B"
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(BASE)
SEP = tok.encode("\n", add_special_tokens=False)          # [198]

def tokenize_row(ex, max_length=512):
    ids = tok(ex["prompt"] + "\n", add_special_tokens=False)["input_ids"]
    labels = [-100] * len(ids)
    for step, ok in zip(ex["completions"], ex["labels"]):
        s = tok(step, add_special_tokens=False)["input_ids"] + SEP
        ids += s
        labels += [-100] * (len(s) - 1) + [int(ok)]  # label on the separator only
    return {"input_ids": ids[:max_length], "labels": labels[:max_length]}

ds = load_dataset("trl-lib/math_shepherd", split="train")
ds = ds.shuffle(seed=0).select(range(4000))
ds = ds.map(tokenize_row, remove_columns=ds.column_names,   # explicit int64, else
    features=Features({"input_ids": Sequence(Value("int64")),  # labels stay bool
                       "labels": Sequence(Value("int64"))}))   # and -100 becomes True

model = AutoModelForTokenClassification.from_pretrained(BASE, num_labels=2)
model.config.pad_token_id = tok.pad_token_id
args = TrainingArguments("prm-out", per_device_train_batch_size=4,
    gradient_accumulation_steps=2, learning_rate=2e-5, num_train_epochs=1,
    warmup_steps=20, gradient_checkpointing=True, report_to="none")
Trainer(model=model, args=args, train_dataset=ds,
        data_collator=DataCollatorForTokenClassification(tok)).train()

blocks.md: For scale: 4,000 rows is about 1% of Math-Shepherd. TRL's documentation showed a quick-start run on the first 10% of it across 8 GPUs, but the model TRL published, `trl-lib/Qwen2-0.5B-Reward-Math-Sheperd` (spelling theirs; the repo now redirects to `trl-archive`), was trained on the whole training split: its training log records 6,601 steps of 64 rows (8 GPUs x 8), about 422,000 rows, roughly 100 times our data. It is built on Qwen2-0.5B and is used below as a comparison.

A bug from our first run. Without `features=`, `datasets.map` kept the input's boolean type for the reused `labels` column, so every -100 became True and the model was trained to call nearly every token correct. Two numbers disagreed: the logged loss was near 0.03, yet cross-entropy measured on the separators alone was 0.58. Printing the mapped labels showed True where -100 belonged. Explicit int64 features fixed it (TRL's trainer passes them too). Every number below is from the fixed run.

The fixed run left a smaller puzzle. Its logged loss ended near 1.25, above the 0.69 of a coin flip, while the saved model's per-separator cross-entropy was 0.557 on 200 of its own training rows and 0.579 on 300 test-split rows. The cause is bookkeeping in the Transformers version used (5.24): the Qwen2 token classifier accepts extra keyword arguments, so `Trainer` passes it the label count of both accumulated micro-batches, assumes the loss was divided by it and skips dividing by 2, but the classifier ignores that count and returns a plain mean per micro-batch. The logged loss is a sum of two means, about twice the real one. Halved, the last four logs read 0.61 to 0.64. The remaining gap of 0.05 to 0.08 has ordinary causes: in a one-epoch run each batch is scored before the model trains on it, so the log is closer to the test-split 0.579 than to 0.557; each log averages different batches; and it weights each micro-batch, not each separator, equally. The gradient doubles too, but logged gradient norms (34 to 264) were far above the clipping limit of 1, so clipping cancels it.

blocks.caption: Scoring: one forward pass, read P(correct) at each separator, reduce. Same tokenization as training.

blocks.md: The test: the first 100 GSM8K test problems, 16 solutions each sampled from Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (temperature 0.8, top-p 0.95) with a prompt asking for *Step k:* lines and a final *The answer is: N*. (The small model sometimes copied the literal N; the answer was then taken as the last number in the solution.) Each sample is split into steps at its *Step* lines and scored. Four ways to pick one answer, all from lesson 6: majority vote, best-of-16 by the minimum or the product of step scores, and PRM-weighted voting (sum of minimum scores per answer).

blocks.title: Picking 1 of 16 samples on 100 GSM8K problems

scenes.caption: A random sample is right 26.5% of the time, and 79% of problems have at least one right answer among 16: the ceiling for any selection rule. Majority vote reaches 46%.

Our 4,000-row PRM: best-of-16 by minimum step score picks a right answer for only 23% of problems, below majority vote and even below a random sample. PRM-weighted voting (minimum scores summed per answer) gets 47%.

TRL's published 0.5B PRM, trained on the full training split (about 100 times our rows): best-of-16 43%, weighted vote 53%. Its weighted vote is the only rule above majority vote, and that 7-point gap is under two standard errors.

blocks.md: Read the bars with care: 100 problems give a standard error of about 5 points, so only large gaps mean anything. Our PRM made best-of-16 *worse* than majority vote (23% versus 46%, below even a random sample at 26.5%), and weighted voting gave 47%, within noise of majority vote. TRL's published PRM, trained with the same labeling on all 422,422 Math-Shepherd rows (8 GPUs, learning rate 1e-5, no separator after the prompt, on Qwen2 rather than Qwen2.5), did better: 43% best-of-16 and 53% weighted, though its best-of-16 still did not beat majority vote. That fits data size mattering, but two models cannot prove it. The lesson 6 advice holds here: weighted voting, which lets the PRM break ties among frequent answers, is the safest way to use a weak PRM.

Two step-level checks tell more. First, on 300 rows of Math-Shepherd's test split (solutions neither model trained on, but not new problems: 299 of the 300 problems also appear in the training split, 36 of them in our 4,000 rows and all 299 in the rows TRL trained on) our PRM's per-separator cross-entropy was 0.579 with 69.7% step accuracy, against 0.692 and 52.1% for a constant guess at the base rate (52.1% of steps are labeled correct); TRL's scored 0.352 and 83.4%, helped by having trained on other solutions to nearly every one of these problems. Ours learned something, not much. Second, the lesson 7 check: across 1,542 scored samples with at least two steps, our PRM put its lowest score on the **final** step 93.3% of the time (TRL's: 73.7%). It mostly reacts to the answer, like an ORM.

Then ProcessBench's GSM8K subset (lesson 7: 207 flawed and 193 correct solutions with a human-marked earliest error; F1 is the harmonic mean of accuracy on each kind). The predicted error is the earliest step the PRM calls wrong; for a 2-way classifier like ours that means P(correct) below 0.5, which is how ProcessBench reads classifier PRMs such as Math-Shepherd's. At 0.5 ours scores F1 0: it flags some step in every correct solution (acc_err 0.222, acc_corr 0). TRL's scores 0.352 (acc_err 0.222, acc_corr 0.845). ProcessBench tunes a threshold only for PRMs that output bare scores, picking the best F1 on this GSM8K subset. Tuned that way on these same 400 solutions, ours reaches 0.147 (threshold 0.13) and TRL's 0.455 (threshold 0.68), but tuning on the test set flatters both, so read those as upper bounds.

blocks.prompt: At threshold 0.5 our PRM flagged an error in all 193 correct ProcessBench GSM8K solutions, though it beats the base rate on Math-Shepherd steps. Its median step score there was 0.61. Name two things that could explain it.
blocks.reveal: First, distribution shift (lesson 7): Math-Shepherd steps are short lines that start with *Step k:* and end in *The answer is: N*, while ProcessBench steps are paragraphs from twelve Qwen and Llama models with no step prefixes, so our PRM's scores there sit near the middle and many fall below 0.5. Second, the decision rule: a solution is flagged if *any* step dips below the threshold, so with several steps per solution, uncertain scores almost guarantee a flag. Lowering the threshold to 0.13 helps only a little (F1 0.147). TRL's model, trained on about 100 times more rows, scores these steps higher (median 0.83) and separates the two kinds better (F1 0.352 at 0.5, 0.455 tuned).

blocks.md: A PRM is a token classifier whose labels sit only on step separators; the rest of the sequence is ignored by the loss. Train and score with identical tokenization, then judge it two ways: does it pick better answers, and does it find the first wrong step.

blocks.question: You train a PRM where every token of a step (not just the separator) carries the step's label. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; more labeled tokens means more signal
The loss can no longer be cross-entropy
Separators stop being tokenized
Tokens early in a step are trained to predict the verdict of text they have not seen yet, and long steps dominate the loss
blocks.explain: A causal model at an early token has not read the rest of the step, so it would be trained to guess a label that depends on future tokens, and steps with many tokens would weigh more. Putting the label only on the separator asks for the verdict once the whole step is visible.

blocks.question: Your PRM scores well on best-of-N reranking but its lowest step score usually falls on the last step. What does that suggest?
options: It mostly judges the final answer, behaving like an outcome model, and may not locate errors
It is a perfect process model, since errors always appear at the end
The product reduction is broken
The step separator was tokenized wrongly
blocks.explain: Errors usually start before the last step. A PRM whose minimum sits on the final step is reacting to the answer, as the Qwen team found for many open PRMs (lesson 7). Checking step-level error location, for example with ProcessBench, tells the two apart.

lessons.title: Step labels without humans: Monte Carlo rollouts

blocks.md: PRM800K needed human experts to read every step. Math-Shepherd (Wang et al., 2023) replaces them with a **completer**: a model that, given a solution prefix ending at step $s_i$, samples $N$ continuations (rollouts) to a final answer. A step is judged by its *potential*: how often continuations from it reach the reference answer $a^*$. Estimating a probability by drawing random samples and counting outcomes is called Monte Carlo (MC) estimation, after the casino, so these are MC step labels. In the paper the completer was LLemma-7B, an open 7-billion-parameter math model, with $N = 8$.

blocks.tex: y^{\mathrm{SE}}_{s_i} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N} \mathbb{1}[a_j = a^*] \qquad y^{\mathrm{HE}}_{s_i} = \begin{cases} 1 & \exists j:\ a_j = a^* \\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}
blocks.caption: Soft estimation (SE) is the fraction of rollouts that reach the right answer. Hard estimation (HE) is 1 if any rollout does. Math-Shepherd trained its PRM on HE labels.

blocks.title: Labeling a 5-step solution with 8 rollouts per step

scenes.caption: A 5-step solution whose first error (known to us, not to the labeler) is step 3. From each prefix the completer samples 8 continuations.
Count rollouts that reach the reference answer: 6, 5, 1, 0, 0. After step 3 the completer can still occasionally repair the mistake, so step 3 gets 1 hit.
Soft labels: 6/8 = 0.75, 0.625, 0.125, 0, 0. They measure how likely this policy is to finish correctly from here, not whether the step itself is right.

Hard labels: 1, 1, 1, 0, 0. The single lucky rollout makes HE call the wrong step 3 correct, so the first error is placed one step too late. Green marks a label that matches the truth, red a wrong label.

blocks.md: The noise in the last scene is systematic, and it depends on $N$. Use a simplified model: rollouts are independent; from a wrong step the completer recovers the right answer with probability $r$; from a correct step it finishes correctly with probability $q$. From a wrong step each rollout misses with probability $1-r$, and independent misses multiply, so all $N$ miss with probability $(1-r)^{\,N}$. HE calls the step good unless every rollout misses, so it mislabels a wrong step as good with probability one minus that, $1-(1-r)^{\,N}$. A correct step is called bad only when all $N$ rollouts fail, which happens with probability $(1-q)^{\,N}$.

blocks.title: Hard-estimation label errors versus rollouts per step

params.name: r
params.label: recovery prob after a wrong step

params.name: q
params.label: success prob after a correct step

scenes.caption: Simplified independent-rollout model. With r = 0.05 and q = 0.3, at N = 8 a wrong step is labeled good 34% of the time and a correct step labeled bad 6% of the time.
More rollouts shrink false negatives but grow false positives: at N = 64 a wrong step is called good 96% of the time. Math-Shepherd saw HE accuracy fall as N grew past 4.
A weak completer (q = 0.05) on a hard problem: correct steps get labeled bad 66% of the time at N = 8. Label quality depends on the completer's strength.

blocks.md: Rolling out from every step costs $k \times M$ completions for an $M$-step solution with $k$ rollouts each. OmegaPRM (Luo et al., Google DeepMind, 2024) only needs the **first** error, so it binary-searches: roll out from the midpoint; if any rollout succeeds the error is in the second half, otherwise in the first. Each round of $k$ rollouts halves the range of candidate steps, and a range of $M$ steps can be halved about log base 2 of $M$ times, so the cost is $O(k \log M)$ rollouts. With $M = 16$ and $k = 8$, brute force costs 16 x 8 = 128 rollouts; binary search needs log base 2 of 16 = 4 rounds (16 to 8 to 4 to 2 to 1), about 4 x 8 = 32. The search assumes success is **monotone** along the solution: *some rollout succeeds* is true for every prefix before the first error and false for every prefix after it. The lucky recoveries shown above break that, and can send the search the wrong way; OmegaPRM accepts this risk in exchange for the $O(k \log M)$ cost. OmegaPRM reused the rollouts in a tree search and collected over 1.5 million annotations.

blocks.title: Binary search for the first error, and how noise misleads it

scenes.caption: An 8-step solution whose first error is step 5. Monotone case: every prefix before step 5 has a successful rollout, none from step 5 on. The search only sees the steps it probes.
Round 1 probes step 4: a rollout succeeds, so the first error is in steps 5 to 8.
Round 2 probes step 6: no rollout succeeds, so the error is in steps 5 to 6. Round 3 probes step 5: no success. First error = step 5 after 3 rounds (log base 2 of 8), not 8.

Noisy case: the completer happens to repair the mistake from step 6 (a lucky recovery). Round 2 now sees success at 6 and searches 7 to 8; round 3 finds no success at 7. The first error is placed at 7, two steps late, and steps 5 and 6 are labeled correct.

blocks.md: Monte Carlo labels estimate a **value** (the chance this policy finishes correctly from here), not step correctness. A 2025 study by the Qwen team (Alibaba's makers of the Qwen models) argues this is the core flaw: a correct step can score low because the completer is weak, and a wrong step can score high because the completer repairs it. They found MC-labeled PRMs worse than ones trained on human labels or on LLM-as-a-judge labels (a strong LLM prompted to check each step) at locating errors.

The same study found that if you do use MC labels, treat a step as correct when **any** of 8 rollouts succeeds (a success-fraction threshold of 0, which is HE), train with hard rather than soft labels, and keep only steps where MC estimation and an LLM judge agree on the error location (*consensus filtering*). Their consensus-filtered PRM matched the LLM-judge PRM using 40% of the data.

blocks.question: You double the number of rollouts per step from 8 to 16 to 'make the labels more accurate', using hard estimation. Which error grows?
options: Correct steps labeled bad, because more rollouts mean more failures
Wrong steps labeled good, because more rollouts give a lucky recovery more chances to occur
Neither; HE labels converge to the truth as N grows
Both shrink equally
blocks.explain: HE marks a step good if any rollout succeeds. P(at least one recovery) = 1 - (1-r)^N rises with N, so wrong steps get marked good more often. Correct-step false negatives (1-q)^N fall. Math-Shepherd observed exactly this: larger N led to false positives.

blocks.question: A step is mathematically correct, but its soft-estimation label is 0.125 (1 of 8 rollouts succeeded). What is the best explanation?
options: The step is subtly wrong; SE is never low for correct steps
Soft labels are always one eighth of hard labels
The completer rarely finishes this hard problem correctly, so SE measures the policy's success chance, not step correctness
The reference answer must be wrong
blocks.explain: SE is a Monte Carlo value estimate for the completer's policy. On a hard problem even correct prefixes rarely finish well. This is the PRM-versus-value-model confusion the Qwen team identified.

lessons.title: What should a step reward measure? Value, progress, implicit PRMs

blocks.md: Lesson 4 warned: a Monte Carlo label says how likely the policy is to finish correctly *from here*, which is not the same as whether the step was right. This lesson takes that seriously and asks what number a step reward should be. Three candidates appear: the **value** of the prefix (the MC label itself), the **progress** a step makes (how much it changes that value), and an **implicit** reward read out of a language model trained only on final-answer labels.

Start with the 5-step solution from lesson 4, whose soft labels were 0.75, 0.625, 0.125, 0, 0. Add one more number: before any step is written, rollouts from the bare question succeed 4 times out of 8, so the empty prefix has value 0.5 (an illustrative count, like the others). **Progress** is the change in value across a step: value after the step minus value before it. Step 1 lifts the chance of success from 0.5 to 0.75, a progress of +0.25.

blocks.title: Value versus progress on the lesson 4 solution

scenes.caption: Value after each prefix (soft labels from lesson 4), plus the empty prefix at 0.5. Values fall gradually, so no single cell shouts where the error is.
Hard labels put the first 0 at step 4: the one lucky rollout after step 3 makes HE call the wrong step correct, as lesson 4 showed.
Progress = value after minus value before: +0.25, -0.125, -0.5, -0.125, 0. Step 3 stands out at -0.5, the largest drop, so the faulty step is located correctly.
Caveat: correct step 2 also gets -0.125, one rollout out of 8. Progress inherits MC noise; with 8 rollouts a one-hit difference is noise, a four-hit drop is signal.

blocks.md: Setlur et al. (2024, *Rewarding Progress*) make this the definition. Write $Q(s, a)$ for the chance of a correct final answer after taking step $a$ from prefix $s$ (the value of the longer prefix) and $V(s)$ for the average of $Q$ over the steps the policy might take. The **advantage** $A = Q - V$ is the progress the step makes. A *value* answers how promising the prefix is; an *advantage* answers whether this particular step helped. They call verifiers trained to predict it **process advantage verifiers (PAVs)**.

blocks.tex: A^{\mu}(s_h, a_h) = Q^{\mu}(s_h, a_h) - V^{\mu}(s_h) \qquad \text{score}(s_h, a_h) = Q^{\pi}(s_h, a_h) + \alpha\, A^{\mu}(s_h, a_h)
blocks.caption: Left: progress of step a_h from prefix s_h, measured with a prover policy mu. Right: the effective reward used for beam search and RL: the base policy's value plus a weighted progress term (alpha is tuned).

blocks.md: Why not rank by value alone? An example in the style of theirs (values illustrative, the -0.05 and +0.20 effects are theirs): prefix A has value 0.80 and its next step drops it to 0.75 (progress -0.05); prefix B has value 0.40 and its next step lifts it to 0.60 (progress +0.20). Ranking by value keeps A's step, a step that made things worse, because A started high. Value mixes two things, how good the prefix already was and how good this step is; the paper says it fails to decouple the *evaluation* of a step from the *promise* of the previous state.

blocks.title: Ranking two candidate steps by Q + alpha A

scenes.caption: alpha = 0, value only: A's step scores 0.75, B's 0.60. Beam search keeps the step that lowered the chance of success.
alpha = 0.5: 0.75 - 0.025 = 0.725 versus 0.60 + 0.10 = 0.70. Nearly tied; the tie point is alpha = 0.6.
alpha = 1: 0.70 versus 0.80. The step that made progress now wins, while the value term still favours prefixes already likely to succeed.

blocks.md: The superscript $\mu$ matters. Progress is measured under a **prover** policy $\mu$ that differs from the policy $\pi$ being trained. Setlur et al. show that with $\mu = \pi$, the advantages add nothing to RL beyond the outcome reward, and that for a weak base policy $Q^{\pi}$ is close to 0 almost everywhere, so its advantages are near 0 too. The prover must be *complementary*: a very weak prover rarely succeeds from any step, and a very strong one succeeds from every step, and either way it cannot tell good steps from bad. Best-of-K samples of the base policy worked well (best-of-4 was their default prover for every base size), and a weaker 9B prover beat a 27B prover for a 27B base.

Reported results: beam search against PAVs was more than 8% more accurate and 1.5 to 5 times more compute-efficient than reranking with an ORM, and online RL with dense PAV rewards gave a 5 to 6 times gain in sample efficiency and more than 6% higher accuracy than RL with an ORM.

blocks.prompt: You train with RL and use your own policy as the prover: the step reward is the change in your policy's own success chance. The outcome reward is still added. Do you expect a large gain over outcome-only RL?
blocks.reveal: No. Setlur et al. show that advantages under the base policy itself give the same policy gradient as the outcome reward alone: the step rewards telescope back to what the final answer already says. The gain comes from measuring progress with a *different*, complementary prover, whose success chances move in ways the base policy's do not.

blocks.md: A different route skips step labels entirely. The **implicit PRM** (Yuan et al., 2024) trains an outcome model whose reward is a log-likelihood ratio, $r_\theta(y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y)}$, from response-level labels only. Here $\pi_\theta$ is the reward model itself, a language model whose weights $\theta$ are trained, $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is a frozen reference copy and $\beta$ a scale. This is the same reward form that falls out of DPO (Direct Preference Optimization, which tunes a model directly on preference pairs; the dpo-variants course, not a prerequisite here, covers it); Yuan et al. show it can be trained with DPO, KTO, NCA or a plain cross-entropy loss on correct and incorrect responses.

A language model's log-probability of a response is a sum of per-token log-probabilities, so the log ratio splits into one term per token. Define the running sum up to token $t$ as $q^t$. Yuan et al. prove that $q^t$ is an expected outcome reward for that prefix, the Q value of the prefix, averaged over continuations drawn from the reference model. The difference $q^t - q^{t-1}$ then says how much token $t$ moved that expectation, which is a process reward, and summing the differences inside a step gives a step reward.

blocks.tex: q^{t} = \sum_{i=1}^{t} \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_i \mid y_{<i})}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_i \mid y_{<i})} = \beta \log \mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid y_{\le t})}\!\left[ e^{\,r_\theta(y)/\beta} \right], \qquad r^{t} = q^{t} - q^{t-1}
blocks.caption: Yuan et al., Proposition 3.1. The expectation is over full responses that start with the first t tokens and continue under the reference model. It is a soft (exponential) average of the final reward.

blocks.title: Checking the identity on a two-step toy (beta = 0.5)

scenes.caption: Two steps, two choices each. The reference picks every option with probability 0.5; the trained model picks a with 0.8, then c with 0.9 after a, and d with 0.7 after b. Response probabilities are the products.
Outcome rewards r = 0.5 log(pi_theta / pi_ref): ac 0.529, ad -0.570, bc -0.714, bd -0.290. Only these four numbers were ever trained against labels.
Running sum after step 1 alone: q = 0.5 log(0.8 / 0.5) = 0.235 for prefix a, 0.5 log(0.2 / 0.5) = -0.458 for prefix b.

The other side: 0.5 log(0.5 e^(0.529/0.5) + 0.5 e^(-0.570/0.5)) = 0.235 for a and -0.458 for b. Equal, as the identity says. A plain average of r would give -0.020 and -0.502: the soft average leans toward the best continuation.
Step 2 rewards are differences: ac gets 0.529 - 0.235 = +0.294, ad gets -0.805. Step d after a is blamed sharply even though no step label was ever given.

blocks.md: Why it holds, in one line for this toy: inside the expectation, $e^{r/\beta}$ is just $\pi_\theta(y)/\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y)$. Weighting by $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ of the continuation cancels the continuation's reference probability and leaves $\frac{\pi_\theta(y_1)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_1)}$ times the sum of $\pi_\theta$ over continuations, which is 1. Taking $\beta \log$ gives back the running sum. Yuan et al. prove the general case by induction over tokens. They trained on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with $\beta = 0.05$ and report that Math-Shepherd's MC labeling cost about 38.8 times more FLOPs than their cross-entropy implicit PRM, with comparable or better best-of-N accuracy on MATH-500.

**PRIME** (Process Reinforcement through IMplicit rEwards, Cui et al., 2025) uses this inside RL. The policy, the implicit PRM and the reference all start from the same SFT model, so there is no separate PRM training stage. Each iteration, the PRM is updated **online** with a cross-entropy loss on the outcome labels of the fresh rollouts, so it tracks the policy's current distribution. Token rewards $\beta \log \frac{\pi_\phi}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}$ ($\beta = 0.05$) and the outcome reward each get a leave-one-out baseline (the mean over the other samples for the same prompt), are turned into returns separately and added, then fed to a PPO-style clipped loss.

In their experiments an offline (frozen) PRM's accuracy fell during RL while the online one improved, which the authors credit for avoiding reward hacking. Eurus-2-7B-PRIME, trained from Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Base, improved 15.1% on average over its SFT model across key reasoning benchmarks and surpassed Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct on seven reasoning benchmarks using 10% of its training data.

An implicit PRM's step reward is a difference of soft Q values under the *reference* model's continuations, learned from outcome labels. It is not a human judgement of the step, and like MC labels it measures how a step changes the expected outcome, not whether the step is mathematically valid.

Value says how promising a prefix is; progress (an advantage) says whether this step helped. Progress is the better step reward, if measured under a complementary prover. Implicit PRMs get Q values for free from an outcome model trained as a log ratio, and PRIME keeps that model fresh with online updates.

blocks.question: Prefix X has value 0.9 and its next step brings it to 0.85; prefix Y has value 0.3 and its next step brings it to 0.5. Which statement is right?
options: The step from X is better because its resulting value is higher
Both steps are equally good because both prefixes are kept by beam search
The step from Y made progress (+0.2) and the step from X lost ground (-0.05); value alone ranks them the wrong way
Progress cannot be computed without human step labels
blocks.explain: Value after the step (0.85 versus 0.5) mixes how good the prefix already was with how good the step is. Progress, the change in value, isolates the step. Setlur et al. use exactly this kind of example to argue for advantages.

blocks.question: In an implicit PRM, what is the step reward for step t?
options: The PRM's sigmoid output at the step's last token
The sum of beta log(pi_theta / pi_ref) over the tokens inside step t, which equals the change in the soft Q value across the step
The fraction of reference-model rollouts from step t that reach the right answer
beta times the step's length in tokens
blocks.explain: The running sum of token log ratios is a soft Q value of the prefix (Yuan et al., Proposition 3.1). Its change across a step, which is the sum of the token terms inside the step, is the step's process reward. No rollouts or step labels are needed.

lessons.title: Using a PRM: reranking, step-level search and RL

blocks.md: A trained PRM is used in three places. **Reranking**: sample N full solutions and pick one by score. **Search**: score partial solutions as they are generated and spend compute on the promising ones. **RL**: use step scores as dense rewards for the policy, a reward at every step instead of only at the end. Each uses the same per-step scores in a different way.

For reranking there is a choice beyond taking the top-scored solution. **Weighted voting** (Li et al., 2023; used by Math-Shepherd and Snell et al.) groups solutions by final answer and sums their scores, picking the answer with the largest total. It mixes the PRM with self-consistency (Wang et al., 2022), the research name for the lesson 1 majority vote over sampled answers. A worked example with six samples:

blocks.title: Three selection rules, three different answers

scenes.caption: Majority vote counts samples: 20 appears 3 times, 24 twice, 17 once. Majority picks 20.
Best-of-N by top single score: the 17 sample scores 0.90, above 0.70 and 0.12. Best-of-N picks 17.
Weighted vote sums PRM scores per answer: 20 has 0.10+0.12+0.08 = 0.30, 24 has 0.70+0.65 = 1.35, 17 has 0.90. Weighted voting picks 24.

blocks.md: **Beam search** uses the PRM on partial solutions. Snell et al. (2024) keep a budget of $N$ beams and a beam width $M$: sample $N$ first steps, score each prefix with the PRM, keep the top $N/M$, sample $M$ next steps from each (back to $N$ prefixes), and repeat until solutions finish (at most 40 rounds). The figure uses $N = 4$, $M = 2$. Beyond beam search, tree search goes further: rStar-Math (Guan et al., 2025) runs Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) guided by a process preference model and reports Qwen2.5-Math-7B rising from 58.8% to 90.0% on MATH.

blocks.title: PRM-guided beam search with N = 4, M = 2

scenes.caption: Sample N = 4 candidate first steps from the policy.
The PRM scores each prefix (illustrative scores). Keep the top N/M = 2: 1a (0.81) and 1c (0.66). 1b and 1d are pruned.
Each survivor gets M = 2 sampled next steps, restoring 4 prefixes. Compute per round stays at N step samples.
Score again and keep the top 2: 2a (0.74) and 2c (0.71). A prefix that was second-best (1c) can still produce a winner.

blocks.md: Snell et al. found that beam search clearly beat best-of-N at small budgets but the gains shrank, and sometimes reversed, at large budgets. To measure difficulty they sorted test problems into five levels by how often the base model solved them (level 1 easiest, level 5 hardest). By difficulty, beam search helped on medium-hard problems but **hurt** on easy ones as the budget grew: a stronger optimizer amplifies the PRM's spurious preferences. Choosing the method per difficulty (*compute-optimal* scaling) roughly matched or beat best-of-N while using up to 4x less test-time compute.

For **RL**, DeepSeekMath (Shao et al., 2024) wrote down process supervision for GRPO. A PRM scores the end of every step $j$ of every output $i$ in the group, giving rewards $r_i^{(j)}$ (the bracketed $j$ is a step index, not a power). All step rewards in the group are normalized together, and each token's advantage is the sum of normalized rewards of the steps at or after it:

blocks.caption: Each step reward minus the mean of all step rewards in the group R, divided by their standard deviation; t is a token position; index(j) is the last token of step j. A token's advantage only counts the steps from its own onward.

blocks.title: Process-supervised GRPO advantages for a group of 2

scenes.caption: PRM step rewards for two sampled outputs: output 1 has 3 steps, output 2 has 2. The 5 rewards have mean 0.7 and (population) standard deviation 0.261.
Normalize every step reward with the group mean and std: 0.9 becomes 0.77, 0.8 becomes 0.38, 0.7 becomes 0, 0.2 becomes -1.92.
Advantage = sum from this step to the end. Output 1: 1.15, 0.38, 0. Output 2: -1.15, -1.92. Both first steps scored 0.9, yet output 2's is pushed down by its bad second step.

blocks.md: Math-Shepherd did the analogous thing with PPO, giving a reward at the end of each step. In the grpo-rlvr course PPO saw one reward, on the last token; with a PRM the per-token reward sequence instead carries the step score on the last token of each step and 0 elsewhere (plus the usual per-token KL penalty). GAE is unchanged: it sums discounted surprises from each token onward, so a token sees the rewards of its own step and all later ones, through the critic's value estimates. It raised Mistral-7B (an open 7-billion-parameter model from the French company Mistral) from 77.9% to 84.1% on GSM8K and 28.6% to 33.0% on MATH, and adding PRM reranking on top reached 89.1% and 43.5%. DeepSeekMath reported process-supervised GRPO beating outcome-supervised GRPO in its experiments.

blocks.title: Where PRM step rewards sit in PPO's per-token rewards

scenes.caption: Two steps of three tokens. Outcome-only PPO would have a single reward on token 6. With a PRM, step 1's score 0.9 sits on token 3 and step 2's 0.2 on token 6 (illustrative scores, KL term left out).

With gamma = lambda = 1, GAE reduces to return-to-go minus the critic's value. Tokens of step 1 see 0.9 + 0.2 = 1.1; tokens of step 2 see only 0.2. The critic's value then decides how much of that was expected.

blocks.md: Dense rewards from a learned PRM come with a specific failure. Gao et al. (2024, *On Designing Effective RL Reward at Training Time for LLM Reasoning*) added ORM or PRM rewards to the success reward in PPO on MATH and GSM8K and found they often failed to help and sometimes hurt. With PRM rewards summed over steps, generation length and the number of steps rose sharply during training: the policy learned to emit short, correct but useless steps, at the extreme a single word, each of which the PRM scored well. In synthetic tests, repeating a step or writing filler such as *Step done.* earned very large returns.

blocks.title: Summed PRM reward: 3 steps versus the same padded to 6

scenes.caption: Every step scores 0.9 (illustrative). Raw summed reward: 2.7 versus 5.4. Padding doubles the return without making the answer any better.

Delta: each step gets its score minus the next step's, the second-to-last keeps its own and the last step's is dropped (the success reward covers it). The sum telescopes to the first step's score: 0.9 for both lengths.

blocks.md: **Clip** takes the other route: subtract a threshold and cap at 0, so no step reward is ever positive. With an illustrative threshold of 0.95, each 0.9 step gets min(0.9 - 0.95, 0) = -0.05, so 3 steps sum to -0.15 and 6 steps to -0.30: extra steps can only cost. Gao et al. prove that with Delta the return from any step equals (a scaled) PRM score of that step plus the success reward, so it is bounded.

blocks.tex: \text{Clip: } r_k = \min(r^{\mathrm{PRM}}_k - \eta,\ 0) \qquad \text{Delta: } r_k = r^{\mathrm{PRM}}_k - r^{\mathrm{PRM}}_{k+1}\ (k < K-1),\quad r_{K-1} = r^{\mathrm{PRM}}_{K-1},\quad r_K = 0
blocks.caption: Gao et al.'s two refinements (K is the last step; Delta drops its PRM reward because the success reward already covers it). Both bound the total reward any trajectory can collect, so length stops paying. eta is a threshold the paper does not fix.

blocks.md: Combining Clip and Delta with the success reward, they report improvements across 1.5B and 7B models on MATH and GSM8K, including for Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct (greedy MATH 83.30 to 83.38, a small gain; the large gain they report under sampling is footnoted as partly the base model producing strange characters). The same hazard is the general reward hacking met in the grpo-rlvr course: the optimizer finds whatever the reward model over-credits, and here that is the number of steps.

Same scores, three uses: rerank finished solutions (weighted voting is a strong default), prune partial solutions in beam search (best on harder problems at modest budgets), or provide step-level rewards so RL can credit each step separately.

blocks.question: With a PRM, beam search beats best-of-N on medium-hard MATH problems (levels 3 and 4) but loses on easy ones as the budget grows. What explains the easy-problem loss?
options: On easy problems the PRM is mostly right already, so stronger search mainly exploits its spurious preferences
Beam search uses fewer samples than best-of-N at the same budget
Easy problems have fewer steps, so the PRM cannot score them
Weighted voting is disabled in beam search
blocks.explain: Snell et al. interpret it this way: on easy questions the verifier is mostly correct, so extra optimization amplifies its errors (e.g. repetitive or overly short solutions). On harder questions the base model rarely samples the right path, so guidance helps.

blocks.question: In process-supervised GRPO, two outputs have identical first steps with the same PRM reward. Why can their first-step tokens get opposite-sign advantages?
options: Normalization uses a different mean per output
The KL penalty differs between the outputs
Each token's advantage sums the normalized rewards of its own step and all later steps, so later steps differ
Only the last step's reward matters
blocks.explain: The advantage for a token is the sum of normalized step rewards at or after its step. In the example both first steps normalize to 0.77, but output 2's later step (-1.92) makes its first-step advantage -1.15.

blocks.question: Your PPO run with a summed PRM reward shows mean response length doubling while accuracy stays flat. Which fix bounds the problem?
options: Raise the PRM's learning rate so it adapts faster
Switch the reduction from product to minimum at inference
Use more rollouts per step when labeling
Reward each step with its PRM score minus the next step's (Delta), so a trajectory's total reward is bounded by one step's score
blocks.explain: Summed per-step rewards grow with the number of steps, so padding pays. Delta makes the sum telescope to the first step's score; Clip makes every step reward non-positive. Both cap the return of any trajectory (Gao et al., 2024).

lessons.title: Failure modes, evaluation, and why some labs skip PRMs

blocks.md: A PRM is a learned model being optimized against, so everything known about reward-model over-optimization applies, at every step: push hard enough against a learned reward and its score keeps rising while true quality stalls or falls, because the optimizer finds the reward model's mistakes. Snell et al. saw search exploit their PRM by producing low-information repetitive steps, or solutions only 1 to 2 steps long. **Distribution shift**, scoring samples unlike the ones a model was trained on, also bites: they found a PRM trained on PRM800K (GPT-4 samples) easy to exploit with samples from their own model, Google's PaLM 2, even with plain best-of-N, and fell back to Monte Carlo labels on their own policy.

Evaluation is its own trap. Most papers judge a PRM by best-of-N accuracy, which only checks final answers. The same Qwen team from lesson 4 manually checked correct-answer responses from Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct and found that a sizeable share had flawed steps: 5.1% on GSM8K rising to 43.4% on Omni-MATH, a set of olympiad-level competition problems. A PRM that rightly penalizes those looks *worse* on best-of-N. They also found many existing PRMs put their minimum score on the final answer step, behaving like an ORM.

**ProcessBench** (Zheng et al., Qwen, 2024) tests error location directly: 3,400 solutions, mostly to competition and olympiad-level problems (its four subsets are GSM8K, MATH, and two olympiad-level sets, OlympiadBench and Omni-MATH), with human-annotated earliest error. The model must output the index of the earliest wrong step, or say all steps are correct. The score per subset is the harmonic mean (F1) of accuracy on erroneous samples and accuracy on correct samples. The harmonic mean of $a$ and $b$ is $2ab/(a+b)$, the reciprocal of the average of their reciprocals; it stays close to the smaller of the two, so a grader cannot hide a bad score on one side behind a good one. F1 is the name this mean has in information retrieval, where it combines precision and recall.

blocks.caption: acc_err: fraction of flawed solutions where the exact earliest error step is found. acc_corr: fraction of fully correct solutions declared correct.

blocks.prompt: A lazy 'PRM' says every solution is fully correct. On a ProcessBench subset with equal numbers of flawed and correct solutions, what is its plain accuracy, and what is its F1?
blocks.reveal: Plain accuracy is 50%: it is right on every correct solution and wrong on every flawed one. F1 is **0**, because acc_err = 0 and the harmonic mean collapses when either term is 0. That is why the benchmark uses F1: it punishes both never flagging errors and flagging everything.

blocks.title: ProcessBench F1 for four hypothetical graders

scenes.caption: acc_corr per grader: 1.0, 0.3, 0.2, 0.8. Judged only on correct solutions, the lazy grader looks perfect.
acc_err (exact earliest step found): 0, 0.4, 0.9, 0.6. The trigger-happy grader flags early and often, so it catches most errors.
F1: 0, 0.343, 0.327, 0.686. Only the grader that is good at both wins; extreme behaviour in either direction is penalized.

blocks.md: ProcessBench's main finding was that existing open PRMs generalized poorly beyond GSM8K and MATH and were beaten by simply prompting strong general models to critique each step, and by a PRM fine-tuned on PRM800K.

DeepSeek-R1 (2025) listed PRMs among its unsuccessful attempts, giving three reasons: a fine-grained **step** is hard to define for general reasoning; judging whether an intermediate step is correct is hard (automatic labels are poor, manual labels do not scale); and a model-based PRM invites **reward hacking**, while retraining it adds cost and complexity. They concluded PRMs help for reranking and guided search, but their benefit in large-scale RL did not justify the overhead, and they used rule-based outcome rewards instead.

One response to these objections avoids step labels altogether: the **implicit PRM** of lesson 5, which reads step rewards out of an outcome model trained as a log-likelihood ratio, and PRIME, which updates it online from outcome labels during RL so that it tracks the policy. Another response, generative verifiers that reason before judging, is the subject of the next lesson.

Do not judge a PRM only by best-of-N accuracy. That metric checks final answers, rewards PRMs that act like outcome models, and depends on which generator produced the samples. Check step-level error location (for example ProcessBench) on the distribution you will actually run it on.

PRMs give denser, more precise feedback than outcome checks, but they are learned models: they can be exploited by search and RL, they degrade under distribution shift, and their labels (human, MC, or judge) each carry their own noise. Use them where search or reranking pays off and keep the final-answer verifier in the loop.

blocks.question: A team reports their new PRM raised best-of-64 accuracy on GSM8K by 0.3 points over an ORM. What is the strongest reason to doubt that it locates errors well?
options: Best-of-N only checks final answers, so a PRM that scores like an outcome model can do well without finding step errors
0.3 points is always within noise for GSM8K
GSM8K problems have no intermediate steps
PRMs cannot be compared with ORMs
blocks.explain: The Qwen team showed best-of-N misaligns with process verification: many correct-answer responses contain flawed steps, and existing PRMs often concentrate their minimum score on the final step. A step-level benchmark such as ProcessBench tests error location directly.

blocks.question: Which of these was NOT one of DeepSeek-R1's stated reasons for not using a PRM in large-scale RL?
options: Defining a fine-grained step in general reasoning is hard
Judging intermediate-step correctness is hard, and manual labels do not scale
A model-based PRM leads to reward hacking and retraining adds overhead
PRMs cannot rerank top-N responses or assist guided search
blocks.explain: DeepSeek-R1 says the opposite: PRMs show good ability to rerank top-N responses and assist guided search. Their objection was that the benefit in large-scale RL did not outweigh the extra compute and complexity.

lessons.title: Generative PRMs: verifiers that reason before they judge

blocks.md: Every PRM so far is **discriminative**: it reads the solution and, at each step's last token, outputs one probability from a classification head. It cannot think before answering; whatever checking it does has to happen inside a single forward pass. Lesson 7 reported a hint that this is a limit: on ProcessBench, strong general models simply *prompted to critique each step* beat the open PRMs of the time. A **generative verifier** turns that observation into a trained model.

Take solution 3 of the shirt problem from lesson 1: discount 10, then tax computed on 40 instead of the 30 sale price (3.2), then an addition slip that happens to land on 32.4. A discriminative PRM returns numbers. A generative verifier returns text like the critique below, and the numbers are read off the text.

blocks.caption: Illustrative critique in the per-step format ThinkPRM is trained to write (the wording is ours; the boxed verdict per step and the final question follow the paper's format).

blocks.title: Discriminative versus generative step scoring

scenes.caption: Discriminative PRM: one forward pass, one probability at each step's separator (illustrative numbers). Cheap, but step 2's flaw only shows as a middling 0.88.
Generative verifier: the same model family writes a step-by-step check first. Its verdicts come after reasoning about each step, and it names the faulty step.

For ranking, the verifier is asked 'Is the solution correct?' and the score is the probability of Yes. For ProcessBench, the first step boxed incorrect is the predicted earliest error: step index 1 here (0-based). The Yes probability shown is illustrative.
Cost is the price: the top path costs one pass over the solution; the bottom path decodes a long chain. ThinkPRM allows up to 8192 verification tokens per solution.

blocks.md: **GenRM** (Zhang et al., Google DeepMind, 2024) introduced the recipe. The verifier is trained with ordinary next-token prediction, on verification and on solution generation together. The direct version is asked *Is the answer correct (Yes/No)?* and its score is the probability of the Yes token. The chain-of-thought version (GenRM-CoT) first writes a verification rationale, then answers Yes or No. Because the rationale is sampled, you can sample K of them and average the Yes probabilities, a majority vote over verifications that spends more test-time compute on checking. The paper's default is K = 32.

blocks.tex: r_{\text{MajV@}K}(x, y) = \frac{1}{K} \sum_{i=1}^{K} p_\theta\!\left(\text{Yes} \mid x, y, v^{(i)}, I\right), \qquad v^{(i)} \sim p_\theta(\cdot \mid x, y, I_{\text{CoT}})
blocks.caption: x is the problem, y the solution, I the Yes/No question, and v the sampled rationales. GenRM fine-tunes open Gemma models; with best-of-N on GSM8K the paper reports 73% to 93.4%.

blocks.md: **ThinkPRM** (Khalifa et al., 2025) applies this to step-level checking with long chain-of-thought models. Starting from R1-Distill-Qwen models (1.5B, 7B and 14B; the main results use 1.5B and 14B), it fine-tunes on about 1,000 verification chains covering roughly 8,000 step labels, which is 1% of PRM800K's process labels. The chains were sampled from QwQ-32B-Preview critiquing PRM800K solutions and kept only if every step had a parsable verdict that matched the human label; about 20% passed. Fine-tuning reduced, for most models, the failure modes of prompted judges: unparsable output, overthinking and loops.

blocks.title: ProcessBench F1 (OmniMath subset): prompted judge vs ThinkPRM

scenes.caption: Same R1-Distill-Qwen base, prompted as an LLM judge versus fine-tuned as ThinkPRM (Khalifa et al., Table 3). The prompted 1.5B model scores 5.4 F1, mostly because its outputs often cannot be parsed.
OlympiadBench subset tells the same story: 5.0 to 76.3, 44.8 to 73.4, 72.8 to 87.3. A thousand filtered chains are enough to turn a reasoning model into a usable step checker.

blocks.md: ThinkPRM beat discriminative PRMs and LLM-as-a-judge baselines under best-of-N and reward-guided search on MATH-500 and AIME 2024. Out of domain, on subsets of GPQA-Diamond (science questions) and LiveCodeBench (coding), it beat discriminative verifiers trained on the full PRM800K by 8% and 4.5%. At an equal token budget it scaled verification compute better than LLM-as-a-judge, by 7.2% on a ProcessBench subset.

**GenPRM** (Zhao et al., 2025) adds code: the verifier reasons in chain of thought and writes and runs code to check a step's arithmetic before judging it. Its labels come from a *relative progress estimation* scheme, close in spirit to the progress idea of lesson 5. Trained on 23K examples from MATH, the authors report that with test-time scaling (several verifications voted) a 1.5B GenPRM beats GPT-4o and a 7B GenPRM beats Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-72B on ProcessBench, and that the critiques can guide the policy to refine its answer.

blocks.prompt: ThinkPRM's scores come from the probability of a Yes or No token after a long chain. Do you expect them to be well spread between 0 and 1, like a calibrated probability?
blocks.reveal: No. The authors report **overconfidence**: scores cluster near 0 or 1, because after a long chain that has already decided, the final Yes or No token is nearly certain. They also report **step label interference**: once the chain judges a step incorrect, later steps become more likely to be judged incorrect too. Both matter for reranking, where ties near 1 must be broken, and for RL, where a reward that is almost always 0 or 1 carries little more than an outcome check.

blocks.md:
How to choose, along four axes:

- **Cost per verification**: discriminative PRMs need one forward pass; generative ones decode hundreds to thousands of tokens, and voting multiplies that by K.
- **Labels needed**: discriminative PRMs want large step-labeled sets (PRM800K, or millions of MC labels); ThinkPRM needed 1% of PRM800K, but its filtering still relied on gold step labels.
- **Calibration**: discriminative step probabilities are graded; generative scores cluster near 0 and 1.
- **Use in RL**: scoring every rollout with a long verification chain multiplies rollout cost, so cheap discriminative or implicit PRMs remain the usual choice inside the training loop, while generative verifiers shine for reranking, search and evaluation.

A generative verifier is an LLM judge that was trained for the job. For further reading beyond this course's prerequisites: the biases of prompted judges (position, length, self-preference) are covered in the llm-as-judge course, and verifier design for agents, such as cascades and false positive rates, in agent-verification.

Generative PRMs phrase verification as text generation: write a step-by-step critique, then read the verdicts and a Yes probability off it. They need far fewer labels and lead on error location, at the price of many more tokens per verification and overconfident scores.

blocks.question: A team wants a step-level verifier for best-of-16 reranking on olympiad math and has only a few thousand step labels. Which choice fits best?
options: A long-CoT generative verifier fine-tuned on filtered verification chains, accepting the higher cost per verification
A discriminative PRM trained on the few thousand labels
Hard-estimation MC labels with N = 64 to remove noise
Product reduction of an ORM's scores
blocks.explain: ThinkPRM reached strong ProcessBench F1 from about 8K step labels by starting from a reasoning model and training it to write verification chains. A discriminative PRM needs far more labels, and more MC rollouts make hard labels more optimistic (lesson 4), not cleaner.

blocks.question: Why are generative verifiers less common than discriminative or implicit PRMs as the dense reward inside large-scale RL?
options: They cannot produce step-level verdicts
Their scores are always better calibrated, so dense rewards are unnecessary
Each verification decodes a long chain (and voting multiplies it), which multiplies the cost of every rollout
They require a reference model at inference time
blocks.explain: A discriminative PRM scores a rollout in one forward pass, an implicit PRM in one pass of two models. A generative verifier writes hundreds to thousands of tokens per rollout. Inside RL every rollout must be scored, so that cost dominates.
